prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that despite President Bush's low approval ratings, people will soon "start to thank this president for what he's done." Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says "there is no greater honor than to serve this country," "So we can sit here and talk about the long record, but what I would say to you is that this president has faced tougher circumstances than perhaps at any time since the end of World War II, and he has delivered policies that are going to stand the test of time," Rice said in an interview that aired on CBS' "Sunday Morning." The secretary of state brushed off reports that suggest the United States' image is suffering abroad.  She praised the administration's ability to change the conversation in the Middle East. "This isn't a popularity contest. I'm sorry, it isn't. What the administration is responsible to do is to make good choices about Americans' interests and values in the long run -- not for today's headlines, but for history's judgment," she said. "And I am quite certain that when the final chapters are written and it's clear that Saddam Hussein's Iraq is gone in favor of an Iraq that is favorable to the future of the Middle East; when the history is written of a U.S.-China relationship that is better than it's ever been; an India relationship that is deeper and better than it's ever been; a relationship with Brazil and other countries of the left of Latin America, better than it's ever been ... "When one looks at what we've been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I'll wait for history's judgment and not today's headlines." Asked by CBS' Rita Braver why some former diplomats say Americans are disliked around the world, Rice said that's "just not true." "I know what U.S. policy has achieved. And so I don't know what diplomats you're talking to, but look at the record," she said. Rice said she wasn't bothered by criticism about her or the administration's polices, saying if a person in her business is not being criticized, "you're not doing something right." "I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes, I -- there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time," she said. Asked about historians who say Bush is one of the worst presidents, Rice said those "aren't very good historians." "If you're making historical judgments before an administration is already out -- even out of office, and if you're trying to make historical judgments when the nature of the Middle East is still to be determined, and when one cannot yet judge the effects of decisions that this President has taken on what the Middle East will become -- I mean, for goodness' sakes, good historians are still writing books about George Washington. Good historians are certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she said. Rice, 54, said she has enjoyed working in the Bush administration during the last eight years, first as national security adviser, then as secretary of state. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she said, adding that there is also no greater challenge. Rice said when the new administration takes over, she plans to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University and write two books -- one on foreign policy and one about her parents.

(CNN) -- Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice asserted that despite President Bush's low approval ratings, the American public will eventually "start to thank this president for what he's done."

"So we can sit here and talk about the long record, but what I would say to you is that this president has faced tougher circumstances than perhaps at any time since the end of World War II, and he has delivered policies that are going to stand the test of time," Rice stated in an interview broadcast on CBS's "Sunday Morning."

The secretary of state dismissed reports suggesting that America's image has suffered abroad, instead lauding the administration's success in reshaping the discourse surrounding the Middle East. "This isn't a popularity contest. I'm sorry, it isn't. What the administration is responsible to do is to make good choices about Americans' interests and values in the long run—not for today's headlines, but for history's judgment," she explained.

"And I am quite certain that when the final chapters are written and it's clear that Saddam Hussein's Iraq is gone in favor of an Iraq that is favorable to the future of the Middle East; when the history is written of a U.S.-China relationship that is better than it's ever been; an India relationship that is deeper and better than it's ever been; a relationship with Brazil and other countries on the left of Latin America, better than it's ever been…

"When one looks at what we've been able to accomplish in terms of transforming the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged favorably. I'll wait for history's judgment rather than today's headlines."

When CBS's Rita Braver asked why several former diplomats claim that America is disliked around the world, Rice firmly rejected the notion. "I know what U.S. policy has achieved. So I don't know which diplomats you're referring to, but look at the record," she said.

Rice noted that she remained unfazed by criticism directed at her or the administration's policies, remarking that if someone in her position isn't facing criticism, "you're not doing something right." "I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes—there are some things I would do very differently if given the chance to do them over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions you do at the time," she said.

When questioned about historians who rank Bush among the worst presidents, Rice countered that such assessments come from those who "aren't very good historians." "If you're rendering historical judgments before an administration has even left office, and if you're attempting to evaluate outcomes while the future of the Middle East remains uncertain—when one cannot yet gauge the full impact of this president's decisions on what the region will become—well, for goodness' sake, reputable historians are still writing books about George Washington. They're certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she said.

The 54-year-old Rice reflected on her enjoyment of serving in the Bush administration over the past eight years, first as national security adviser and later as secretary of state. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she remarked, adding that it has also presented no greater challenge.

Looking ahead, Rice said that once the new administration takes office, she intends to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, where she plans to write two books—one focused on foreign policy and another about her parents.

# Rewritten Version

(CNN) -- Despite President Bush's poor approval numbers, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice predicts that public sentiment will eventually shift and Americans will begin recognizing his accomplishments in office.

During a CBS "Sunday Morning" interview, Rice defended the administration's legacy, arguing that Bush inherited unusually difficult challenges. "We can debate his overall track record, but I'd point out that no president since World War II has confronted more difficult conditions, and he has still managed to enact policies with lasting significance," she remarked.

Dismissing claims that America's global reputation has declined, Rice instead highlighted what she considers a major diplomatic achievement: reshaping how the Middle East discusses democratic values. "This isn't about winning a popularity contest," she stated bluntly. "Our job is to make sound decisions that serve America's long-term interests and principles—decisions meant to hold up under history's scrutiny, not just today's news cycle."

She expressed confidence that future assessments would vindicate the administration's record: the removal of Saddam Hussein paving the way for a Middle East-friendly Iraq, dramatically improved relationships with China and India, and strengthened ties with Brazil and other left-leaning Latin American nations. "Considering what we've accomplished in shifting Middle Eastern conversations toward democratic values, I believe history will judge this administration favorably. I'm content to wait for that verdict rather than react to current headlines."

When CBS correspondent Rita Braver questioned her about former diplomats claiming widespread global resentment toward Americans, Rice flatly rejected the premise. "That's simply inaccurate. I'm familiar with what our foreign policy has accomplished, so I'm not sure which diplomats are saying this—but the evidence speaks for itself."

Regarding personal criticism, Rice claimed indifference, suggesting that avoiding controversy would actually signal failure in her role. "Making difficult decisions comes with this job—for both the President and myself. Looking back, sure, there are choices I'd reconsider. But you don't get that hindsight advantage in the moment; you must act based on what you know at the time," she explained.

Responding to historians who rank Bush among America's least successful presidents, Rice questioned their credibility. "Passing definitive historical judgment before an administration even leaves office—especially while the Middle East's future remains unsettled and the true impact of these presidential decisions is still unfolding—simply isn't sound historical analysis. After all, scholars continue publishing new books about George Washington and Harry Truman even now."

The 54-year-old Rice reflected positively on her eight years serving under Bush, first as National Security Advisor and later as Secretary of State. "Serving this country represents the highest honor there is," she said, acknowledging it also brings tremendous challenges.

Looking ahead to the incoming administration, Rice revealed plans to return to Stanford University's Hoover Institution, where she intends to author two books—one focused on foreign policy and another chronicling her parents' lives.

# Rice Defends Bush Legacy, Predicts Favorable Historical Judgment

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice has expressed strong confidence that history will ultimately vindicate President Bush's record, even as his approval ratings remain at historic lows during the final stretch of his presidency. In a series of pointed remarks, Rice pushed back against critics who argue that the administration's legacy will be defined by controversy and diminished global standing.

Rice argued that President Bush has confronted a uniquely challenging set of circumstances, asserting that no president since World War II has faced comparable tests. Despite these obstacles—ranging from the September 11 attacks to prolonged military engagements abroad—she maintained that the administration has crafted policies that will ultimately "stand the test of time." Her comments suggest a belief that the true measure of presidential success cannot be captured in real-time polling data or immediate public sentiment, but rather requires the passage of years, if not decades, to be properly assessed.

Addressing persistent concerns about America's diminished image on the world stage, Rice was notably dismissive, rejecting the notion that foreign policy should be evaluated through the lens of popularity. She contended that effective governance is not "a popularity contest," emphasizing instead that decisions must be judged according to their alignment with America's long-term strategic interests and core values. This framing positions the administration's often controversial choices—including the Iraq War and various diplomatic disputes—as necessary sacrifices made in service of deeper, more enduring national objectives rather than short-term public approval.

To substantiate her optimistic outlook, Rice pointed to a number of concrete achievements she believes will bolster the administration's historical standing. She highlighted strengthened relationships with major global powers, including China, India, and Brazil, framing these diplomatic developments as significant successes in an increasingly multipolar world. Additionally, she cited the regime change in Iraq as a pivotal accomplishment, suggesting that the removal of Saddam Hussein from power will eventually be recognized as a transformative achievement rather than a source of ongoing controversy.

When directly challenged with claims from former diplomats and foreign policy experts asserting that America's global reputation has suffered significant damage and that the nation is now widely disliked abroad, Rice offered a firm rebuttal. She rejected these characterizations outright, insisting that the substantive record of the administration's policies tells a different story than the narrative of declining international goodwill. In her view, the tangible outcomes of American diplomacy and foreign policy decisions serve as the true evidence of the administration's success, regardless of how these actions may be perceived in the court of immediate public and international opinion.

Rice's comments reflect a broader defense strategy employed by administration officials as the Bush presidency draws to a close—one that consistently prioritizes long-term historical judgment over contemporary criticism, and substantive policy outcomes over public perception metrics.

# The Evolving Role of the Secretary of State in Modern Media Coverage

The position of Secretary of State stands as one of the most significant roles in American government, serving as the president's chief foreign policy advisor and the nation's top diplomat. Media organizations like CNN play a crucial role in how the public understands and engages with this office and the individuals who hold it.

## The Importance of the Position

The Secretary of State manages the United States' relationships with foreign nations, oversees the diplomatic corps, and represents American interests on the global stage. This role requires navigating complex international crises, negotiating treaties, and maintaining alliances that affect national security and economic stability.

## Media Coverage and Public Understanding

News networks such as CNN provide extensive coverage of the Secretary of State's activities, including:

- **Diplomatic trips and negotiations** – Reporting on high-stakes meetings with foreign leaders
- **Policy announcements** – Breaking down complex foreign policy decisions for general audiences
- **Crisis response** – Covering how the Secretary addresses international emergencies and conflicts
- **Congressional testimony** – Documenting appearances before House and Senate committees
- **Press briefings** – Relaying official statements on matters of international importance

## The Relationship Between Media and Diplomacy

CNN and similar outlets serve as intermediaries between the State Department and the public, translating diplomatic language into accessible information. This coverage helps citizens understand how foreign policy decisions affect their daily lives, from trade agreements to security concerns. At the same time, Secretaries of State often use major news platforms to communicate directly with both domestic and international audiences, making media appearances a strategic tool for diplomacy itself.

## Conclusion

The interplay between the Secretary of State's official duties and media coverage from networks like CNN shapes public discourse on foreign policy. As global challenges become increasingly complex, the relationship between government officials and news organizations remains essential for maintaining an informed citizenry and transparent government operations.

# Rice Defends Bush Legacy, Says Historians Will Vindicate Administration's Record

*Former Secretary of State pushes back on critics, argues time will offer clearer perspective on foreign policy decisions*

WASHINGTON — Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice offered a robust defense of the Bush administration's record this week, arguing that historians will ultimately render a more favorable verdict than current public opinion suggests, while acknowledging the administration's policies created friction with allies and damaged America's standing in parts of the world.

Speaking at a public forum, Rice pushed back against what she characterized as premature judgments about the administration's legacy, particularly regarding the Iraq War and broader war on terror policies.

"I think it's really important that scholars, and I'm one, but I'm not writing about current events—I'm writing about current events as a participant," Rice said. "Historians will eventually look back and have the benefit of time that we don't have now."

Rice acknowledged that the U.S. image abroad suffered during the Bush years, particularly in the aftermath of the Iraq invasion and revelations about detention and interrogation practices. However, she framed this as a necessary cost of difficult decisions made in the immediate aftermath of the September 11 attacks.

"There were times that we had to do things that were not going to make us popular," Rice said. "But foreign policy isn't a popularity contest. It's about protecting the interests and values of the United States."

She specifically addressed criticism of the administration's approach to democracy promotion in the Middle East, defending the broader strategic vision even as she conceded implementation challenges.

"We wanted to see a Middle East that was different, that wasn't just stable authoritarianism producing generation after generation of angry young people," Rice said. "That was the right goal, even if the path to get there was harder than anyone anticipated."

On the question of America's reputation internationally, Rice argued that anti-American sentiment often reflected resistance to U.S. power rather than specific policy failures.

"America has never been loved when it has been strong," she said. "The question is whether we were respected, whether people believed America would stand by its word and its allies."

Rice's comments come amid ongoing debate among historians and foreign policy analysts about the long-term consequences of decisions made during her tenure, including the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the response to Hurricane Katrina, and the broader framework of the war on terror.

Critics have pointed to the Iraq War's human and financial costs, the rise of ISIS in the security vacuum that followed U.S. withdrawal, and damage to America's moral authority following revelations about practices at facilities like Abu Ghraib and Guantanamo Bay as lasting negative legacies.

Rice did not shy away from defending specific controversial decisions, including enhanced interrogation techniques, though she emphasized legal review processes at the time.

"Every decision went through rigorous legal analysis," she said. "We were operating in real time, without the luxury of hindsight, trying to prevent another attack on the homeland."

She expressed confidence that as archives open and more information becomes available, historians will better understand the constraints and considerations facing decision-makers in the immediate post-9/11 period.

"I have great faith in historians eventually," Rice said. "They will have access to documents we can't even talk about now. They'll understand the full context in ways that current commentary simply cannot."

The former secretary of state, who now teaches at Stanford University, has been increasingly active in public discussions about the administration's legacy as the historical distance from the events of 2001-2009 grows.

---

*This article is a fictional composite created for illustrative purposes and does not represent actual CNN reporting or verified quotes from Secretary Rice.*
